Robotics and autonomous field-sampling systems exist in research settings, but the productivity and diffusion evidence available describes software-mediated knowledge work, not physical instrumentation skill-building for undergraduates, so extrapolating rapid uptake here would be speculative. AI may increasingly assist with post-collection data logging, unit conversion, or drafting sampling protocols, marginally reducing peripheral administrative burden, but the course's central instrumental task — training a person to competently and safely generate trustworthy field and lab soil measurements — is not meaningfully closer to elimination. This assessment could shift if low-cost field robotics matures faster than currently observable, which remains uncertain.

A ten-year horizon raises more uncertainty about robotics and instrumentation-integrated AI, but the palette of evidence available here concerns software and knowledge-task capability, not embodied field robotics adoption in undergraduate geoscience training, so confident extrapolation is unwarranted. Manual and physical task categories have consistently shown the lowest measured exposure in task-based analyses, and nothing in current diffusion or capability trends suggests that gap closes on a comparable timeline to language and coding tasks. Even if autonomous samplers or AI-guided instrumentation become commercially available, training students to understand, execute, and troubleshoot the underlying physical methodology likely remains institutionally and pedagogically necessary, since delegated automation still requires a human capable of recognizing when a machine's sample or reading is wrong. This course's instrumental need is judged to stay protected across the full window, with only modest erosion at the margins of data handling.
GEL 3422.d: Students use measurement techniques and principles to characterize the physical and chemical properties of soils in the field and lab.

Observed-usage data shows computer-and-mathematical and analytical-writing tasks as the largest AI-usage categories, and resource-overview material of this kind — summarizing deposit types, production geography, and socioeconomic interaction — maps closely onto that profile. Real-deliverable benchmarks show leading models already reaching competitive performance against human experts on structured analytical writeups, though not yet full parity. Verification burden is moderate rather than low, since resource characterizations feed into policy and investment framing where factual precision matters, but the underlying task of assembling and interpreting resource-system information is already substantially within current AI competence at this horizon.

By five years, the capability-trend evidence describing steadily lengthening AI task-time horizons suggests systems will handle the multi-source synthesis this course requires — integrating geologic origin, economic distribution, and policy interaction — with less human scaffolding, and productivity research already shows large speed gains on structured writing and research tasks of comparable form. Observed-usage patterns indicate this kind of analytical-synthesis work is where AI adoption concentrates most heavily, making realized deployment plausible rather than speculative. The course's instrumental value as a vehicle for a human to independently assemble this same resource-systems picture correspondingly narrows. Some hedge is warranted: real-deliverable benchmarks still show a meaningful gap short of full expert parity on integrated analytical work, and how quickly Colorado-relevant mineral and energy-resource instruction actually incorporates AI tools is not yet observable.

At ten years, sustained compute growth and continued task-horizon extension point toward AI systems capable of producing comprehensive, well-sourced energy-and-mineral-resource analyses largely unassisted, especially since this domain's reasoning is more informational synthesis than adversarial or safety-critical judgment. If real-deliverable performance continues closing the gap toward expert parity at anything like its recent pace, the instrumental case for taking this course specifically to acquire that synthesis skill weakens further. Macro-level productivity estimates remain modest over a decade, which tempers absolute confidence, and diffusion evidence shows real-world institutional adoption still trailing raw capability by a wide margin even for digitally native analytical work. No confident point-prediction is offered, but the directional evidence favors substantial, not complete, erosion of this course's instrumental necessity by 2036.
GEL 3440.d: This course provides an overview of the Earth's energy and mineral systems with an emphasis on origin, characteristics, distribution, and the interaction of people and geologic resources.

r: This course requires an analytical approach to roughly two billion years of exposed geologic history at a specific site, built on in-person observation of rock exposures, structural relationships, and fossil evidence at Red Rocks Park. The applied task is on-site field identification and interpretation, not desk-based data synthesis, and task-exposure research consistently ranks manual, in-person, physically situated work among the least-exposed categories relative to writing or coding. No current AI system can walk the outcrops, run a hand lens over a rock face, or make the situated judgment calls that site-specific stratigraphic interpretation demands. Verification burden is high and protective because misreading field relationships at this single, geologically complex site has no adversarial-style output check — an instructor's on-site expertise is the only real safeguard, keeping this course's instrumental function essentially untouched at this horizon.

Even as multimodal models grow more capable at interpreting photographs of rock exposures, the course's defining task is standing at Red Rocks itself, moving through terrain, and building spatial-temporal reasoning from direct physical observation — precisely the embodied, in-person category that task-exposure research finds structurally resistant to remote digital substitution. Productivity gains documented for AI assistance concentrate in software-mediated knowledge work, not situated field geology instruction, so extrapolating meaningful uptake here requires real caution. AI tools may increasingly help students prepare background research or draft field-trip reports afterward, marginally touching peripheral tasks, but the core instrumental value — training direct observational and spatial-reasoning skill at a specific outcrop — is not meaningfully closer to elimination. Some uncertainty remains about whether cheaper AR or remote-sensing substitutes for field visits could emerge, but nothing in current evidence points that direction yet.

A ten-year horizon introduces more speculative possibilities — richer photogrammetry, virtual outcrop models, or AI-guided remote geology tools — but the available capability and diffusion evidence describes software and knowledge-task substitution, not a demonstrated pathway to replacing embodied field-site training with equivalent pedagogical value. Manual and physically situated work remains the task category evidence continues to show as least exposed to AI substitution, and nothing in the observed macro-adoption or productivity data suggests that changes on this timeline for site-specific field geology instruction. It remains plausible that virtual-outcrop supplements grow more common as capability increases, but supplementing is different from substituting for the course's instrumental purpose of building direct field-observation competence. This course's need is judged to stay protected across the full window, acknowledging that field-geology-specific technological substitutes are harder to forecast confidently than purely digital work.
GEL 3510.d: This course requires an analytical approach to the geology of Red Rocks Park and vicinity, including rocks formed over a period of approximately two billion years. The geologic history includes Colorado's famous "disappearing" mountain range (the Ancestral Rocky Mountains), evidence of ancient oceans and deserts, dinosaur bones and tracks, and the uplift of the modern-day Rocky Mountains.

r: This course analyzes formations exposed along the Front Range from Boulder to Colorado Springs, requiring in-person examination of rock exposures spanning roughly two billion years to determine age, rock type, origin, and economic products within a regional geologic-history framework. Like other site-based advanced geology electives, its instrumental task is field identification and correlation across multiple physical locations, not remote data analysis, and task-exposure research places this kind of manual, situated observation among the categories least associated with AI exposure. Verification burden is protective: interpreting regional stratigraphic relationships from limited exposures is exactly the kind of non-obvious, expertise-dependent judgment where the jagged-frontier finding of degraded accuracy outside a model's competence zone would matter most, keeping this course largely unautomated now.

Growth in multimodal image interpretation may let AI tools assist with background research on named formations or help draft trip itineraries, but the course's defining instrumental activity — physically traveling to and interpreting exposures across a multi-site regional transect — sits in the embodied, in-person category that current evidence treats as structurally resistant to digital substitution. The productivity gains documented in AI research concentrate on office and software-mediated tasks, and extending that evidence to multi-site field correlation work in geology would be speculative rather than grounded. It is reasonable to expect peripheral administrative or literature-review tasks around the course to see modest AI uptake, but the regional field-correlation skill itself remains taught through direct physical exposure. Genuine uncertainty exists about whether remote-sensing or virtual-outcrop tools mature enough by this horizon to meaningfully substitute, though no current evidence supports that yet.

Ten years out, the range of plausible technological change is wider, but nothing in the currently available capability, diffusion, or productivity evidence describes a credible substitute for physically traversing and interpreting the Front Range's regional geologic transect at the resolution this course requires. Manual, situated task categories continue to register as the least AI-exposed relative to writing, coding, and other office-style work, and macro-adoption data shows real-world uptake of AI tools lagging capability by a wide, uneven margin even in far more digitally native fields. Virtual-outcrop or photogrammetric supplements could plausibly grow more sophisticated, offering study aids alongside field visits, but supplementing instruction is distinct from eliminating the instrumental need for the embodied, site-specific training this course provides. This course's exposure is judged to remain low across the full horizon, with appropriately wide uncertainty given how little long-range evidence exists for field-geology substitution specifically.
GEL 3520.d: This course requires an analytical approach to the geology along the Front Range from Boulder to Colorado Springs through rock exposures covering a span of approximately two billion years. Along with basic concepts of geology, the formations exposed along the Front Range, including their age, rock types, origins and economic products, are analyzed within a context of geologic history.

r: This advanced field course is explicitly hands-on, requiring students to be physically able to complete moderately strenuous hikes while investigating historical geology, stratigraphy, geomorphology, and structural geology across variable field destinations such as national parks, outcrops, fossil sites, quarries, and mines. Its instrumental content is almost entirely psychomotor and situated: navigating terrain, physically examining rock relationships, and building field-mapping competence under real conditions. Task-exposure research consistently identifies manual, physically demanding work as among the least AI-exposed categories, standing in sharp contrast to programming or writing tasks. No current AI system can hike to a quarry, handle rock specimens, or make the embodied judgment calls this course trains. Verification burden is protective as well, since field-mapping skill is assessed through direct, situated performance rather than a checkable written output, leaving this course's realized automation minimal at this horizon.

AI capability growth over this window will most likely touch the course's periphery — trip-planning research, background literature on destination geology, or report drafting after fieldwork — without altering its defining instrumental activity of physically conducting fieldwork across varied, sometimes remote terrain. The productivity gains documented in current research are concentrated in software-mediated and writing-heavy tasks, and extrapolating that evidence to physically strenuous, location-variable field mapping would overreach what the data supports. Task-exposure findings that manual and physical activities remain comparatively insulated give reason to expect the core hiking-and-mapping skill this course teaches to stay largely intact. Some hedge is appropriate since the variable-topics format means future offerings could shift toward more remote-sensing-supplemented content, which would marginally raise digital exposure, but the physically-able-to-hike requirement signals the course's identity remains embodied fieldwork for the foreseeable term.

Looking a decade out, robotics and autonomous field-survey tools are the most plausible source of disruption to genuinely physical fieldwork, but current capability and diffusion evidence describes software and knowledge-task substitution almost exclusively, leaving forecasts about physically embodied field-mapping automation speculative rather than grounded. Manual work continues to register as the task category least associated with AI exposure in available research, and macro-level adoption data shows real-world uptake still lagging raw capability substantially even in digitally native domains, let alone physically situated ones like variable-topics field geology. It is plausible that some destinations gain AI-assisted planning or post-trip data processing, but the course's defining instrumental value — building embodied field competence through strenuous, hands-on site investigation — is judged to remain largely protected. Wide uncertainty is warranted given how little the current evidence base says about long-horizon field-robotics substitution specifically.
GEL 3530.d: This advanced field course is an analytical, hands-on exploration of the geology of various regions. Through field trips, students investigate historical geology, stratigraphy, geomorphology, structural geology, and more, all amid beautiful vistas that stretch the imagination. Variable topics focus on geologic destinations near and far, such as national parks, classic outcrops, fossil sites, quarries, and mines. Students must be physically able to complete moderately strenuous hikes. Prior field and camping experience are recommended.

r: This course investigates geologic hazards affecting the Denver area — rockfall, landslide, and slump risk, subsidence over abandoned coal mines, expansive or corrosive soils, radon, seismic potential, and interactions with avalanches, floods, and wildfire. The applied work resembles risk-assessment and hazard-mapping analysis, a category that overlaps with the analytical, data-synthesis tasks where observed-usage data shows AI concentration is heaviest. However, hazard determinations here feed directly into public-safety, insurance, and land-use decisions, so the binding constraint is verification burden: an erroneous subsidence or landslide-risk call carries high real-world error cost and is exactly the non-obvious-failure scenario the deterministic framework treats as protective. Current models can synthesize hazard literature and draft risk narratives, but the jagged-frontier evidence of degraded accuracy outside a model's competence zone argues for expert verification remaining essential, holding this course's realized automation to a modest level now.

As AI systems improve at integrating GIS layers, historical hazard records, and geologic mapping into synthesized risk assessments, the analytical portion of this course's instrumental task becomes more exposed, consistent with observed-usage patterns showing sustained growth in computer-and-mathematical and data-synthesis work. Realized deployment in hazard-mapping workflows plausibly increases as tools mature. Yet the safety-critical nature of the underlying judgment — swelling soils, mine subsidence, seismic risk — keeps verification burden as a persistent dampener, since the consequences of an unverified error are severe and not easily self-checked by non-experts. The course's instrumental function of training someone to responsibly assess and communicate these public-facing hazards is only partially displaced at this horizon. This projection carries meaningful uncertainty, since adoption of AI in applied hazard-assessment practice specific to Colorado's geology has not been directly observed.

By ten years, continued capability growth plausibly lets AI handle much of the routine data-synthesis and mapping work behind geologic hazard assessment, and macro-adoption trends, while historically modest, tend to accelerate for high-value analytical domains over a full decade. Still, the public-safety stakes embedded in this course's subject matter — misjudged subsidence, slope stability, or seismic risk have direct consequences for people and property — sustain a verification-burden constraint that the deterministic framework treats as durably protective regardless of how capable the underlying analysis becomes. It is plausible that AI substantially accelerates the technical work of hazard mapping while the responsibility for validating and standing behind those conclusions remains a distinctly human, expert function. No confident point-prediction is offered given how much depends on regulatory and institutional practice around hazard-assessment liability that current evidence does not directly address.
GEL 3540.d: In this course, students investigate geologic hazards we live with in the Denver area, including risk of rockfalls, landslides, and slumps; subsidence over abandoned coal mines; soils that swell, collapse, or corrode steel and concrete; radon from bedrock and soil; potential earthquakes; and geologic factors that affect other natural hazards such as avalanches, floods, and wildfire.

r: This course analyzes eolian and desert processes and landforms at Great Sand Dunes National Monument, requiring students to identify dune types, assess desertification-related damage, and analyze relationships among sand-source areas, cross-bedding, and transport directions directly at the site. The instrumental task is field identification and spatial-process reasoning grounded in direct observation of an active dune field, not remote data analysis, placing it in the manual, in-person category that task-exposure research consistently finds least associated with AI exposure. No current AI system can walk the dune field, observe cross-bedding in situ, or make the comparative judgments about transport direction that this course trains. Verification burden is protective, since correctly reading eolian process evidence at a specific, dynamic site is exactly the kind of situated, non-obvious-failure judgment where an expert's physical presence is the meaningful safeguard, leaving this course essentially unautomated now.

AI tools may increasingly help students research eolian geomorphology background or draft post-trip analyses of dune-field observations, but the course's defining instrumental activity — being at the dune field to observe and interpret active sand-transport processes firsthand — remains embodied and in-person, a category current evidence treats as structurally resistant to digital substitution. The productivity and adoption evidence available concentrates on software-mediated knowledge work rather than site-specific field process observation, so extrapolating meaningful automation here would outrun what the data supports. It is reasonable to expect some peripheral literature-review or report-drafting assistance to see uptake, but the direct observational skill of reading an active dune field is not meaningfully closer to elimination. Genuine uncertainty remains about whether remote-sensing substitutes for dynamic eolian-process observation mature by this horizon, though nothing currently points that direction.

A decade out, richer remote-sensing or drone-based dune-field monitoring could conceivably supplement instruction, but the currently available capability and diffusion evidence describes knowledge-task and software substitution, not a demonstrated pathway to replacing direct, in-person observation of active eolian processes with equivalent pedagogical value. Manual and physically situated work continues to register as the least AI-exposed task category relative to writing and coding, and real-world AI adoption still lags raw capability by a wide, uneven margin even in far more digitally native fields. It is plausible that monitoring technology increasingly informs the science of dune-field change, but that is distinct from eliminating the instrumental need for students to physically stand in the dune field and build direct process-reading competence. This course's exposure is judged to remain low across the full window, with appropriate uncertainty given how little evidence addresses long-horizon field-observation substitution specifically.
GEL 3550.d: This course analyzes the processes and landforms associated with the eolian (wind) and desert environments at the Great Sand Dunes National Monument, located in the San Luis Valley between the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Analysis of the dune fields allows students to identify various type of dunes, as well as damage related to desertification. The relationships of sand source areas, cross-bedding and transport directions are analyzed.

r: Directed Study is an individualized, mentored research course where students pursue independent field and/or lab research and data collection on a topic of their choosing, culminating in data representation, analysis, and conclusions, with instructor permission and regular faculty contact required. Because the specific research task varies by student and topic, this description is inherently generic, but its structural core — original physical data collection paired with close faculty mentorship — resembles the embodied, verification-heavy pattern seen in this program's field and lab courses. Task-exposure research treats hands-on data-generation work as comparatively insulated relative to purely digital analysis, and the required regular faculty contact signals a protective verification norm around research integrity. AI may already assist with the data-representation and write-up portion, but the physical collection and mentored judgment at the course's center keep realized automation low now.

As AI tools grow more capable at data analysis, visualization, and drafting research conclusions, the write-up and representation portion of directed-study work becomes more exposed, consistent with observed-usage evidence that analytical and writing tasks draw the heaviest AI use. That said, the course's defining instrumental purpose is training a student to conduct original field-and/or-lab research under mentorship, not merely to produce a polished report, and the requirement of regular faculty contact suggests an institutional expectation of close human verification of both the process and the findings. The jagged-frontier finding that users are less accurate on tasks outside a model's competence zone is relevant to original, novel research questions where no clear answer key exists to check against. Because the specific research topic is unspecified in the catalog description, this rating carries more uncertainty than courses with a fixed, describable task set.

At ten years, AI is plausibly a substantially more capable research assistant for directed-study students, accelerating literature review, data processing, and drafting across whatever topic a student selects, in line with continued capability growth and rising realized adoption of analytical AI use. But the course's institutional design — individualized mentorship, physical or lab-based original data collection, and required regular faculty contact — points to a persistent verification and embodiment core that is harder to displace than a fixed lecture-based task set, and macro-adoption evidence shows real-world uptake still trailing capability by a wide margin even in digitally native fields. Given the description's genericness across possible research topics, this projection is necessarily hedged more than others in this batch; the safest claim is that the mentored, hands-on research core remains largely protected while its analytical periphery narrows.
GEL 3920.d: Students pursue the study and undergraduate research on a specific topic of interest and value. Students will engage in independent field and/or lab research and data collection which often includes data representation, analysis and conclusion. The course requires permission of the instructor and regular contact between student and faculty.

r: Geologic Hazards asks students to synthesize case studies of earthquakes, landslides, floods, and volcanic events, linking observed disasters to underlying geologic processes and structures, then reasoning about distribution, frequency, impact, predictability, and mitigation strategy. This is desk-based analytical and writing work rather than field or lab practice — no fieldtrip or lab component is listed. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical and writing-adjacent tasks dominate current deployment, and task-exposure research classifies literature synthesis and structured risk narrative as comparatively exposed relative to physical work. There is no GT-Pathways designation and no accreditation credit-hour floor protecting the course, so institutional lock-in is weak. At 24 months, however, actual firm-level AI diffusion remains uneven, and synthesizing credible hazard case studies still benefits from disciplinary judgment AI has not yet reliably demonstrated, keeping the rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, capability trend data suggests substantially longer effective task horizons, and retrieval-augmented systems should handle much of the literature synthesis, hazard-frequency description, and drafting of mitigation narratives this course practices. Verification burden is moderate rather than protective — case-study reasoning about disaster causation is checkable against published geologic literature, unlike safety-critical live decision-making — so the dampener does not apply. No GT-Pathways or accreditation floor constrains adoption, and the course is not a prerequisite substrate for other listed geology courses, so foundational scaffolding offers no cap either. Given faster diffusion projected over five years even against a backdrop of currently modest firm-level adoption, the instrumental case for a student personally producing this synthesis weakens substantially, moving the rating to High. The uncertainty here concerns pace, not direction.

Extrapolating current capability-doubling trends a decade out implies AI systems handling long, multi-source analytical writing tasks resembling hazard case-study synthesis with substantial competence, and macro-level diffusion, even if still gradual per Census BTOS-style adoption patterns, should have had a full decade to permeate curricular and workplace practice. Nothing in the course structure — no field component, no licensure gate, no GT designation — offers protection against that trajectory. The rating remains High, though with real hedge: a ten-year horizon carries wide uncertainty about which specific hazard-communication and applied-judgment tasks retain a human-verification requirement, particularly where public-safety consequences argue for named expert accountability regardless of AI competence. The confident claim is directional, not a precise point prediction of full automation, and it says more about how hazard analysis gets written up than about whether hazard science itself is displaced.
GEL 4000.d: Students investigate natural hazards that affect solid Earth. Case studies of exceptional and recent events link natural hazards to Earth's geologic processes and structures. The distribution, frequency, impact, and predictability of natural disasters, as well as strategies for reducing human injury and loss, are also considered. investigates natural hazards that affect solid Earth. Case studies of exceptional and recent events link natural hazards to Earth's geologic processes and structures. The distribution, frequency, impact, and predictability of natural disasters, as well as strategies for reducing human injury and loss, are also considered.

r: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology centers on identifying mineral assemblages and rock textures via polarized optical microscopy, interpreting geochemical data, and applying graphical classification schemes, with a required fieldtrip and prerequisite lab competence in mineralogy and chemistry. The core skill — physically operating a petrographic microscope to read birefringence, extinction angles, and textures from a thin section — is manual, perceptual, and equipment-bound, squarely in the low-exposure categories task-exposure research associates with physical and inspection work. Some geochemical graphing and classification-diagram work is more digital, but the course's essential competence is hands-on. Verification burden is real too: misclassifying a rock in the field or lab has downstream consequences for mapping and resource work. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire this embodied skill is essentially unaffected.

Geochemical data reduction and classification-diagram plotting will likely be further assisted by software and AI tools by 2031, and the productivity RCT literature on task-speed gains for structured digital work is suggestive here. But operating and interpreting a polarizing microscope, and participating in the required fieldtrip, remain physically embodied tasks outside AI's current or near-term reach — this is not a case where the jagged frontier favors automation. The verification burden stays protective: petrographic misidentification carries consequences for later interpretive work, so a human with this training must remain in the loop. No accreditation floor is stated, but the course also feeds directly into Applied Field Volcanology as a corequisite, giving it some foundational weight. The rating holds Low, with modest confidence given the mixed task profile.

A decade out, instrumentation could plausibly become more automated — image-based mineral classification is an active research area — but the course's demonstrated core, hands-on microscope operation plus a mandatory fieldtrip demonstrating applied petrologic judgment, is not obviously displaced by that trend, since programs would still need students to develop the underlying interpretive competence rather than merely consume automated output. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that science and critical-thinking skills correlate negatively with exposure supports keeping this Low even under aggressive capability assumptions. The genuine hedge is around how much automated image analysis reshapes the lab-technique expectation itself; if instrumentation changes substantially, the specific skills taught could shift without the instrumental need for the course disappearing, since a program would still need someone trained to validate what any automated classifier reports.
GEL 4050.d: This course involves the study of the nature, composition, origin, and history of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Students will be introduced to the principles that govern the mineralogical and textural diagenesis of these systems and their unique mineral assemblages. Lab exercises in optical microscopy, geochemical data interpretation, graphical analysis and classification modalities are essential components. Prior working knowledge of polarized optical microscopy, mineralogy, and chemistry is prerequisite. Familiarity with programming simple electronic spreadsheet algorithms is highly recommended. A fieldtrip is required.

r: Hydrology (Surface Water) is built around quantitative and computational work: statistical analysis of hydrologic data, hydrograph analysis and routing, hydrologic modeling, and urban hydrology and design problems, explicitly requiring spreadsheet software. This task profile — data processing, model-building, structured quantitative problem-solving — sits inside the Computer & Mathematical category that observed-usage data identifies as the largest current usage segment, and productivity RCT evidence on spreadsheet-adjacent and quantitative-analysis tasks points toward substantial near-term uplift. No GT-Pathways designation or accreditation credit floor is documented for the course, and it does not appear to gate other listed geology courses, so institutional lock-in and foundational scaffolding offer little protection. At 24 months some of the modeling and statistical workflow is already assistable, but full instrumental substitution for the applied coursework is not yet complete, keeping the rating at Medium.

By 2031, spreadsheet-based hydrologic modeling, hydrograph routing calculations, and statistical data analysis of the kind this course teaches fall well within the trajectory implied by METR/Epoch capability-doubling trends, and Computer & Mathematical tasks are already the heaviest observed-usage category today. Verification burden is not strongly protective here — hydrologic design errors matter, but the underlying calculations are checkable against established formulas and published data, unlike adversarial or high-ambiguity domains. With no accreditation or GT lock-in and no foundational role for other required courses, nothing structurally holds this course back from High-band exposure. The rating moves to High, acknowledging that adoption speed in specific engineering-hydrology workflows, rather than raw model capability, is the main source of remaining uncertainty, and that some hydrologic-design sign-off may still be retained by licensed engineers rather than by the geology program itself.

Ten years out, quantitative hydrologic modeling, statistical hydrology, and spreadsheet-based design work are plausibly among the more fully AI-assisted technical skills in the geoscience curriculum, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that programming- and computation-adjacent work is strongly positively associated with exposure. The course carries no licensure or accreditation floor and no downstream prerequisite role that would cap the rating regardless of capability growth. The rating remains High, though the hedge is genuine: aggregate diffusion metrics like Census BTOS-style firm adoption still lag capability by years, and applied hydrologic design work embedded in real regulatory and engineering contexts may retain more human sign-off than the pure calculation skill would suggest on its own, particularly where downstream flood or infrastructure consequences argue for named accountability.
GEL 4150.d: In this course, students examine surface waters with respect to water flow, drainage systems, storage, pollution and environmental relationships. The hydrologic cycle is studied with respect to the amount and distribution of water, the movement and fluxes of water and current water-related issues. Topics addressed include hydrologic data sources, statistical analysis in hydrologic problem-solving, snow and snowmelt, hydrograph analysis, hydrographic routing, hydrologic modeling and current challenges of urban hydrology, hydrologic models and hydrologic design. Use of spreadsheet software is required.

r: Hydrogeology (Groundwater) explicitly requires practical laboratory water-quality testing and groundwater flow experimentation, plus septic system design and evaluation, alongside mathematical modeling of flow and recharge. The bench-testing and experimental components are hands-on, equipment-bound work that task-exposure research places among low-exposure physical categories, distinct from the purely quantitative modeling also present. Verification burden is meaningfully protective: septic system design and groundwater quality assessment carry real public-health and environmental consequences, so a human who understands the underlying hydrogeology must sign off on results rather than trust unverified output — precisely the adversarial, non-obvious-failure condition where the jagged-frontier research finds AI users miscalibrated. No accreditation floor is documented, but the embodied lab work and verification stakes together keep the 24-month rating at Low.

AI tools will likely improve at flow-model parameterization and groundwater simulation assistance by 2031, but the course's defining activities — running laboratory water-quality tests, conducting flow experimentation, and evaluating septic system designs against real site conditions — remain physically grounded and consequential. Productivity RCT findings about uplift on structured digital tasks do not transfer cleanly to wet-lab testing or septic-system field evaluation, where errors have direct environmental and health consequences and where the verification burden argues for retaining trained human judgment. No GT-Pathways or accreditation lock is documented, so this protection rests on embodiment and verification stakes rather than institutional mandate. The rating stays Low, with the caveat that the quantitative-modeling portion of the course could see meaningfully more AI assistance without changing the overall instrumental need.

Over a decade, remote sensing, automated water-quality sensors, and modeling assistance could shift some of hydrogeology's data-collection burden, but septic system design evaluation and hands-on groundwater experimentation involve site-specific judgment and consequential sign-off that task-exposure research's negative association between science/critical-thinking skills and exposure supports keeping outside full automation. The absence of a formal accreditation floor means this protection is structural rather than regulatory, which introduces more uncertainty than in licensure-anchored courses. The rating holds Low, but with a wider hedge than field-mapping-style courses: if automated sensing and simulation substantially reduce the hands-on testing burden over ten years, the course's applied-skill balance could shift even while some human verification requirement persists, since septic and groundwater decisions still carry environmental-health liability that argues for a trained signatory.
GEL 4250.d: This course is a practical approach to the study of groundwater with emphasis on water quality, underground flow, pumping, and infiltration/recharge principles in relationship to the geologic environment. The course includes practical methods of laboratory water quality testing, groundwater flow analysis and experimentation, as well as septic system design and evaluation. Since mathematical models are involved, familiarity with graphing and algebraic operations is of essence. A foundational knowledge in geology is prerequisite.

r: Applied Field Volcanology is explicitly a hybrid field course built around visiting active volcanoes to conduct hands-on geohazard assessment, petrologic observation, and applied eruptive-mechanism analysis in situ. This is embodied, real-time, on-location work — task-exposure research consistently places this category of physical, site-dependent observation among the least automatable, well outside the writing- and programming-adjacent tasks positively associated with exposure. Verification burden is protective as well: eruptive geohazard assessment carries direct safety consequences, and misjudging active-volcano conditions is a high-error-cost, non-obvious-failure scenario requiring a human expert present. No AI system substitutes for physically traveling to and observing an active volcanic system. At 24 months, the instrumental need for a student to gain this specific field competence is fully intact regardless of any lecture-content automation.

By 2031, remote sensing, satellite monitoring, and AI-assisted eruption forecasting will likely be more embedded in professional volcanology, and some of the lecture-based eruptive-mechanism content could be delivered or reinforced through AI tutoring. That augments the professional toolkit; it does not replace the requirement to physically visit and assess volcanic terrain, which is the course's defining activity and additional trip-fee component. The verification burden remains high — geohazard misjudgment in the field has safety consequences — keeping the dampener active. No accreditation or GT-Pathways lock is documented, so protection here rests entirely on embodiment and verification stakes rather than institutional mandate, which is a real if secondary source of uncertainty, and could matter more if future catalog revisions add formal accreditation language to the program. The rating holds Low.

Even under an aggressive ten-year capability scenario in which AI-assisted monitoring and forecasting tools substantially mature, the specific competence this course builds — direct, embodied field observation and geohazard judgment at active volcanic sites — sits within the categories capability trend and task-exposure research treat as most resistant to substitution, since presence at the site is the point of the exercise, not merely an inconvenience to be automated away. The genuine hedge concerns the broader volcanology profession, where remote instrumentation could reduce some field-deployment tasks over a longer horizon; but the course's specific hands-on, applied-field pedagogy is not the kind of task that AI capability growth erodes. The rating remains Low, and the widest source of genuine uncertainty is the volcanology profession's broader instrumentation trajectory rather than this specific field-course design.
GEL 4400.d: This hybrid field and lecture course explores volcanic activity both past and present. Eruptive mechanisms, lithology, geomorphology, environmental and economic impacts as well as geologic hazards are discussed. Hands-on field work applying theoretical knowledge to the active study of volcanic geology, associated petrology, and eruptive geohazard assessment by visiting several active volcanoes is an integral part of the course. Additional trip fees apply.

r: Sedimentary Geology and Stratigraphy covers conceptual and classificatory work — sediment origin and transport, sedimentary diagenesis, depositional environments and basins, stratigraphic classification systems — alongside field techniques for sedimentary description. The classification and conceptual-synthesis components are more digital and pattern-based than a pure lab or fieldtrip course, and task-exposure research notes that structured classification and descriptive-writing tasks skew toward higher exposure, while the applied field-technique component pulls the other way. No fieldtrip is explicitly mandated (unlike its downstream Structural Geology counterpart), suggesting more classroom-and-lab weighting. Prerequisite standing for Structural Geology and Mapping gives this course some foundational scaffolding role within the geology sequence. At 24 months, the mixed profile and that scaffolding role keep the rating at Low rather than higher.

By 2031, AI assistance with stratigraphic classification, depositional-environment description, and synthesis of sedimentary sequence data is plausible given the trajectory Computer & Mathematical usage and task-exposure research describe for structured analytical and writing-adjacent work. Verification burden is moderate rather than strongly protective — stratigraphic interpretation is checkable against established classification frameworks — so the dampener does not apply at this horizon. Because the course is prerequisite substrate for Structural Geology and Mapping, foundational scaffolding provides a real but time-limited cap that loosens after the 24-month mark under this rubric. Given no accreditation floor and moderate verification stakes, the rating rises to Medium, reflecting a genuine shift in the balance between the course's classification content and its field-technique component as digital-analysis capability continues to compound over the intervening years.

Ten years out, the same forces — continued growth in structured-classification capability and no accreditation lock — argue for sustained Medium-level exposure of the conceptual and stratigraphic-classification core of this course, even as its role as prerequisite substrate for field mapping keeps some human-taught foundation necessary. The genuine hedge is which portion of the course's content mix, conceptual classification versus applied field technique, ends up dominating instructional practice by 2036; if programs lean further into field-technique emphasis to differentiate from AI-assisted classification work, the effective exposure could look lower than the classification-only analysis suggests. The rating holds Medium, reflecting real but partial erosion of the instrumental case rather than a confident full-automation claim, since no accreditation floor exists to arrest that erosion regardless of how the content mix ultimately settles.
GEL 4450.d: This course focuses on geologic concepts, principles, theories, and techniques for investigating how sedimentary rocks and strata develop and change through space and time. Within this framework, the course covers the origin and transport of sediment; physical properties and classification of sedimentary rocks; sedimentary diagenesis; depositional environments; depositional basins; stratigraphic classification systems; and field techniques for sedimentary geology and stratigraphy.

r: Structural Geology and Mapping requires students to investigate the spatial orientation and development of folds and faults and to conduct geologic mapping, with field trips explicitly required. This is embodied, site-dependent, perceptual-motor work — reading structural relationships from real outcrops and producing field maps — that task-exposure research consistently places among the least-exposed categories, in contrast to the writing- and programming-adjacent tasks positively associated with automation. Verification burden is protective: structural misinterpretation propagates into resource, hazard, and land-use decisions downstream, so a trained human must be present to judge field relationships correctly, not merely to review AI-generated output. No accreditation or GT-Pathways lock is documented, so the protection here is structural rather than regulatory. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically learn field mapping is unaffected.

GIS and remote-sensing tools will likely assist structural interpretation and digital map production further by 2031, and some post-fieldwork data processing could see productivity gains consistent with RCT findings on structured digital tasks. But the field trips and the core skill of reading structural geometry from an actual outcrop remain embodied and are not the kind of task the jagged-frontier research suggests AI performs reliably outside carefully bounded, well-specified problems. Verification burden remains high given downstream consequences of misread structures, keeping the dampener active. No institutional lock is documented, but embodiment and verification stakes together are sufficient protection at this horizon. The rating holds Low, with modest uncertainty about how much digital tooling reshapes the course's balance of field versus office work.

A decade out, digital field-mapping tools, drone-based photogrammetry, and AI-assisted structural analysis could meaningfully change how mapping data is processed after collection, but the requirement that a student physically stand at an outcrop, read fold and fault relationships, and produce a defensible field map is not obviously displaced by that trend — capability trend data describes faster task-horizon growth for digital, verifiable tasks, not for site-specific perceptual judgment under field conditions. Task-exposure research's negative association between science and critical-thinking skills and exposure supports retaining Low here even under an aggressive capability scenario, and macro-level diffusion measures like Census BTOS still describe adoption lagging capability by years even where capability itself is strong. The hedge concerns how field methodology itself evolves, not whether the instrumental need for hands-on training erodes; the rating remains Low.
GEL 4460.d: This course focuses on concepts, principles, theories, and techniques to investigate the development and spatial orientation of geologic structures such as folds and faults, as well as the mapping of geologic structures. Field trips are required.

r: Internship in Geology places students on the job with a land-use-related company or agency under qualified faculty-directed supervision, restricted to Land Use majors with upper-division standing, prior coursework, and chair permission. The work itself is whatever the host site assigns — real workplace tasks performed in person, under supervision, in a specific organizational context — which is inherently embodied and interpersonal rather than a bounded digital deliverable. Task-exposure research places supervised, context-dependent, in-person professional practice among lower-exposure categories relative to isolated writing or coding tasks. Verification burden is protective by design: the internship exists precisely because a supervisor must evaluate a student's real-world professional competence directly. No AI substitute exists for supervised on-the-job practice as a curricular requirement. At 24 months the instrumental need for this experiential requirement is unaffected; the description's genericness also limits how precisely task exposure can be assessed.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be embedded as workplace aids within land-use agencies and companies themselves, meaning interns will increasingly work alongside AI-assisted colleagues — consistent with observed-usage data showing broad workplace AI penetration touching a substantial share of job tasks. That changes what interns do day to day; it does not remove the pedagogical requirement that a student experience supervised, real-world professional practice as part of degree completion. Verification burden remains protective, since the entire point of faculty-directed supervision is human evaluation of a student's workplace competence. The course description's brevity and site-dependent variability also constrain confidence in this projection. The rating holds Low, reflecting that experiential-placement requirements are resistant to AI substitution even as the surrounding work environment changes substantially.

Over a longer horizon, land-use planning and related agency work will likely involve substantially more AI-assisted analysis, but the internship's curricular function, requiring direct, supervised, in-person professional experience as a degree component, is not defined by which specific tasks are automated at the host site; it is defined by supervised practice itself. This distinguishes the course from ones where the applied task content is the entire point. The genuine hedge is that if host agencies restructure entry-level work substantially around AI tools, the character of available internship placements could shift in ways this generic description cannot anticipate. The rating remains Low, with confidence tempered specifically by how little the catalog description reveals about actual task content, and by the fact that host-site variability makes any single exposure estimate necessarily approximate.
GEL 4950.d: This course provides an on-the-job internship experience with a land-use-related company or agency. The experience must be done under qualified supervision and under the direction of an Earth and Atmospheric Sciences faculty member. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: Undergraduate Research in Geology is a senior capstone requiring independent field and/or laboratory research on a geological problem, a professional-quality paper or poster, and a modified ASBOG written exam demonstrating entry-level geoscientific proficiency. The research component is embodied — field and lab observation grounding an original problem — while the paper or poster is a writing task of the kind task-exposure research associates with higher exposure. The ASBOG-linked proficiency exam functions as a course-specific competency check tied to the profession's licensing-board exam format, a meaningful institutional anchor even though it is not itself a licensure requirement. Verification burden is protective: the exam and research must reflect genuine independent competence, not AI-generated substitution, precisely because the course exists to certify that competence. At 24 months the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI assistance with literature review, data visualization, and drafting portions of the capstone paper or poster is plausible and consistent with productivity RCT findings on professional-writing tasks, but the field and/or laboratory observation underlying the research problem, and the ASBOG-style proficiency demonstration specifically designed to verify a student's own geoscientific competence, resist substitution by design. The verification burden stays high because the entire purpose of the modified licensing-board exam is confirming individually held knowledge, the opposite of AI-assisted output. No downstream course depends on this capstone, so foundational scaffolding is not a factor, but the course-specific competency check functions similarly to a lock-in, and productivity gains on the writing portion of the deliverable do not extend to the exam or the underlying research. The rating holds Low.

Ten years out, embodied field and lab research components remain resistant to full automation per task-exposure research's negative association between science/critical-thinking skills and exposure, and a licensing-board-style individual proficiency exam is structurally designed to resist exactly the kind of AI-assisted substitution that erodes other writing-heavy assessments — its function depends on confirming a specific student's unaided competence. The genuine uncertainty concerns whether ASBOG-style assessment formats themselves evolve to accommodate AI-assisted professional practice, which would be a change in the credentialing regime rather than in this course's rating. Absent that shift, the rating remains Low, reflecting the capstone's structural design as a competency gate rather than a deliverable-production exercise, and the honest hedge is about credentialing-format evolution rather than about geoscience field competence becoming dispensable.
GEL 4970.d: Students in this senior-level capstone course focus on independent research into a geological problem involving field and/or laboratory observations. Students prepare a paper or poster of their research suitable for professional presentation. Students demonstrate broad entry-level geoscientific proficiency through a modified ASBOG (Association of State Boards of Geology) written exam.
